item.title: [JAMA_current]💬 Editorial by @JAMAplusTrials Editor in Chief Alison Huang, MD, MAS, and Lehana Thabane, PhD: #ClinicalTrials feasibility research may use prespecified progression thresholds, mixed quantitative and qualitative methods, or internal pilot designs to guide decisions about advancing to larger trials. These approaches can add structure to exploratory research while also leaving room for pilot studies to identify unanticipated barriers, protocol challenges, and design issues not captured by prespecified benchmarks alone. item.title:
[noahatwhere]Researchers write the papers. Reviewers evaluate them for free. Universities and taxpayers fund the research.
And somehow, researchers still have to pay to read the knowledge they collectively produced.
The more you think about it, the more absurd it becomes.
Of course, academic publishing has legitimate costs. But it’s hard to justify a system where access to scientific knowledge depends on whether your institution can afford the subscription.
Science advances through the sharing of knowledge. A system that puts publicly funded research behind paywalls is working against the very purpose of science.
Your ability to do research shouldn’t depend on how much you can afford to pay to read someone else’s.

[PracheeAC]I like the idea of a truly integrated team science funding opportunity. Two threats to success of this new mechanism NIH will have to grapple with:
1) traditional journal publishing 2) fractional time by participants
Winner-take-all first author/last author haggling is incompatible with team science. When you stop playing the journal game as we have done, focus on utility of your research outputs, and focus on responsibility (not just credit) in authorship, you realize how much more smoothly and faster science operates when there’s no implicit bandwidth allocation based on credit ranking.
For similar reasons, having people on the project that operate in a winner-take-all regime with another fraction of their work creates mixed incentives that can starve the collaborative work of maximal tailwind. That liability is in addition to purely operational liabilities from split attention. So I’d recommend most participants on these awards having full-time effort on the collaborative project. Maybe the tangible advancements that are only possible in a collaborative setting and full participation in this collaborative effort could make these team contributors eligible/likely to receive a specific type of follow-on funding or something?
Anyway I applaud the new mechanism and want it to succeed because I think society’s greatest challenges often require the joint contributions of scientists across disciplines. If you have been trying to do research in a truly team setting leveraging diverse expertise (more commonly outside academia), you’ve grappled with this and have seen the upside first hand.

I like the idea of a truly integrated team science funding opportunity. Two threats to success of this new mechanism NIH will have to grapple with:
1) traditional journal publishing 2) fractional time by participants
Winner-take-all first author/last author haggling is incompatible with team science. When you stop playing the journal game as we have done, focus on utility of your research outputs, and focus on responsibility (not just credit) in authorship, you realize how much more smoothly and faster science operates when there’s no implicit bandwidth allocation based on credit ranking.
For similar reasons, having people on the project that operate in a winner-take-all regime with another fraction of their work creates mixed incentives that can starve the collaborative work of maximal tailwind. That liability is in addition to purely operational liabilities from split attention. So I’d recommend most participants on these awards having full-time effort on the collaborative project. Maybe the tangible advancements that are only possible in a collaborative setting and full participation in this collaborative effort could make these team contributors eligible/likely to receive a specific type of follow-on funding or something?
Anyway I applaud the new mechanism and want it to succeed because I think society’s greatest challenges often require the joint contributions of scientists across disciplines. If you have been trying to do research in a truly team setting leveraging diverse expertise (more commonly outside academia), you’ve grappled with this and have seen the upside first hand.
